newsitem.title: BOSNIA: NATO to crack down on Bosnian special police units.
newsitem.headline: NATO to crack down on Bosnian special police units.

text.p: The commander of the NATO-led peace force in Bosnia said on Friday his troops would crack down on unauthorised special police units which had previously escaped the alliance's supervision.

U.S. General Eric Shinseki, the new chief of the Stabilisation Force (SFOR), issued a statement saying special police units which failed to register with international police monitors would be subject to strict controls already imposed on rival armies.
"This policy is designed to assist, accelerate and ensure police restructuring and reform," Shinseki said in the statement.
Western officials said the move was primarily aimed at Bosnian Serb authorities who have refused to restructure their vast police force according to U.N. guidelines.
Some 2,000 to 3,000 special police in Bosnia's Serb territory are controlled by hardliners loyal to indicted war criminal and former Bosnian Serb President Radovan Karadzic.
The anti-terrorist brigade answers to the interior minister, Dragan Kijac, a staunch Karadzic ally who uses elements of the brigade to guard Karadzic.
SFOR and the U.N. mission informed political leaders that special police would be permitted to provide security to senior officials but not to anyone indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal.
Under terms of the peace agreement's military annex, special police units fell under NATO's jurisdiction, but until this week the alliance had chosen to focus on supervising rival armies.

The tougher stance towards special police ratcheted up pressure on hardliners grouped around Karadzic who are already being squeezed by Western governments for their failure to abide by terms of the peace agreement.
Serb authorities were rattled by a NATO raid last month against two Serbs charged with war crimes. One suspect was extradited to the U.N. tribunal and another was shot dead after he resisted arrest.
NATO has issued stern warnings to Serb hardliners who were accused of orchestrating a wave of revenge bombings and attacks against peacekeeping soldiers following the arrest operation.
The move against special police was likely to feed speculation that NATO might decide to snatch Karadzic, who is charged with genocide by the U.N. tribunal for his conduct during the 1992-95 war.
